opus-5.5.text:
I think language is an extraordinarily powerful part of intelligence, but I don't believe it's the essence of it.

Large language models have shown us something remarkable: when you compress enough human text, you get systems that can reason, plan, write code, and talk about almost anything. That's a real breakthrough, and it tells us language encodes a huge amount of human knowledge. But language is a product of intelligence. It's how humans compress and communicate what we've already understood about the world. It isn't the foundation that understanding is built on.

Think about it from an evolutionary perspective. Animals were perceiving, moving, grasping and navigating complex environments for hundreds of millions of years before anything like language appeared. A cat can't talk, but it can judge a jump, land on a narrow ledge and adapt instantly if the surface moves. That's a very sophisticated form of intelligence, and none of it goes through language. Even for humans, a baby learns physics, object permanence and cause and effect by touching, dropping and pushing things long before it can describe any of them.

So from my perspective, working on embodied intelligence, there's a whole layer of intelligence that is physical. It's about interacting with the real world in a closed loop: perceiving, acting, getting feedback and adjusting. Language models are still weak there. They can tell you how to fold a shirt in beautiful prose, but that's very different from controlling the forces and contacts of a robot hand to actually do it. The hard part, the part Moravec pointed out decades ago, is exactly what language doesn't capture well.

Language does play a crucial role, though. It's an excellent interface and a great carrier of high-level knowledge, goals and common sense. In embodied systems we increasingly use language and vision-language models as the "brain" for task understanding and planning. Underneath that, you need a "cerebellum" for perception and motor control, learned from interaction data, simulation and real-world experience.

So my view is that language is one very important pillar of intelligence, maybe the most visible one right now, but general intelligence has to be grounded in the physical world. The next big step isn't just bigger language models. It's connecting them to bodies that can act, so intelligence can learn from the world itself, not only from what humans have written about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes cats and prelinguistic babies as intelligent, showing that intelligence can exist without language.

r002.rationale: It describes a cat’s bodily control and navigation and says language models are weak at physical tasks, but does not compare nonlinguistic organisms with current VRA models.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize purely visual intelligence as difficult to interpret.

r004.rationale: It mentions language compressing knowledge, but not that linguistic communication is efficient because it is compressed into a one-dimensional sequential form.

r005.rationale: It says animals had intelligence before language appeared, but does not characterize language as evolving only at a very advanced level of intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that idea is partly right and partly a trap.

The part that's right: language is probably the most compressed record of human thought we have. When you train a model on a huge amount of text, you're not just learning grammar, you're absorbing an enormous amount of structure about the world that people have already done the work of abstracting. So it's not surprising that language models show capabilities that look a lot like reasoning. Language was never just a communication channel; it was a tool humans built for thinking.

But I come from robotics and embodied intelligence, so I'm always a bit suspicious when people say language is the essence. Think about a child before they can talk. They already know that objects persist when you hide them, that liquids spill, that if you push a cup off the table it falls. None of that came from language. It came from interacting with the physical world, from a body that gets feedback. And a lot of the things we consider "intelligent" in animals, a dog catching a frisbee, a crow using a tool, happen with no language at all.

So my view is that language is more like the interface layer, or maybe the index, of intelligence rather than its substance. It's extremely powerful for transmitting knowledge between people, and now between people and machines. But if you ask a language model to actually fold a towel, or to pick up a cup it's never seen with a hand it's never used, you discover very quickly that a lot of what matters in the world is not written anywhere. It's in the dynamics, the contact, the friction. Nobody writes a paragraph about how much force to apply to a strawberry.

Where I think the two meet is interesting. Language gives you a very good prior, a way to decompose a task, to say "first open the drawer, then take out the spoon." Embodiment gives you the grounding that turns those words into something that actually works in a kitchen. The models that will really look intelligent to us will be the ones where those two things are learned together, where the words are tied to perception and action, not floating on their own.

So, is language the essence of intelligence? I'd say it's the essence of human intelligence's transmissibility. The essence of intelligence itself, I think, is still the ability to act well in a world you don't fully understand. Language is the best tool we've found to help with that. It's not the whole thing.

r001.rationale: It says children and animals show intelligence without language and calls language not the essence of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of animal abilities and language-model limitations, but does not compare nonlinguistic organisms with current VRA models in bodily control and navigation.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize purely visual intelligence or its interpretability.

r004.rationale: It calls language a compressed record of thought, but does not attribute communication efficiency to compression into a one-dimensional sequential form.

r005.rationale: It does not describe language as evolving only at an advanced level of intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think language is an important expression of intelligence, but I’m not sure it’s the essence of intelligence. We use language to describe our reasoning, communicate ideas, and build on what other people have learned. So it’s understandable that we often judge intelligence through language.

But consider what it takes to pick up a cup. You have to perceive its shape, estimate where it is, control your hand, and adjust your grip. You may do all of that without putting anything into words. Babies and animals also learn about the world without having the kind of language we have.

So I would distinguish between language as a powerful tool for thinking and intelligence as the broader ability to learn, predict, and act. Language can capture a great deal of our knowledge about the world, but describing something and being able to do it are different capabilities. For me, the interesting question is how those capabilities connect.

r001.rationale: It describes perception and motor control, and learning by babies and animals, as intelligent activity that can occur without words.

r002.rationale: It mentions bodily control and animals, but makes no comparison to current VRA models or claim that nonlinguistic organisms may exceed them.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss purely visual intelligence or how difficult it is to interpret.

r004.rationale: It says language helps people communicate and build on knowledge, but does not attribute its efficiency to compression into a sequential form.

r005.rationale: It does not characterize language as evolving only after intelligence reached an advanced level.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is an important expression of intelligence, but calling it the essence of intelligence may be too strong. We use language to organize ideas, communicate, and reason about abstract things, so it’s easy to see intelligence through that lens. But perception, spatial reasoning, and learning how to act in the physical world also involve intelligence, and they don’t necessarily depend on language.

Think about a child learning to pick up an object. There’s an understanding of space, motion, and cause and effect developing before the child can explain any of it. Language later helps make that understanding explicit and shareable.

So I would distinguish between language as a powerful tool for intelligence and language as its foundation. The interesting question is how language connects with perception and action—whether a system can connect what it says to what it observes and does.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize visual intelligence as difficult to interpret.

r004.rationale: It does not explain linguistic communication's efficiency in terms of one-dimensional sequential compression.

r005.rationale: It does not describe language as emerging only at an advanced level of intelligence.
